text.p: British tour operator Airtours Plc, which reported record pre-tax profits on Wednesday, said it was prepared to spend up to 250 million stg on one or more strategic acquistions.

Chairman and chief executive David Crossland told Reuters that the company was quite keen on boosting its cruising business, buying a new U.S. or Canadian company or on finding another country in Europe where it could have a similar business to those it already has in Scandinavia and Britain.
"We're probably in a position to spend between about 200 and 250 million stg on the right sort of acquisition," he said.

"We have the resources to be able to do that today...We have very specific areas that we're looking to," he noted, adding that the company had a very strong balance sheet and year in cash of about 425 million pounds.

Airtours, which sells tours to holiday makers in Britain, Scandinavia and Canada, said it believed there would be significant opportunities for further expansion which it would "exploit as they arise".
Airtours, which has seen pretax profits surge from six million stg in 1990 to 86.8 million stg today, has spent about 240 million stg on acquisitions over that period.

"We shall seek to develop or acquire businesses operating in markets which we understand, where we can add value and where the acquired business has high quality management or alternatively can be readily integrated into our existing mangement infrastructures," the company stated.

Despite carrying about 12 percent less passengers in summer 1996 than in the previous year, Crossland said Airtours had been able to raise profits in its UK business by 50.2 percent to 41.8 million stg by persuading passengers to buy more expensive holidays.

Summer 1997 will see about the same number of packages as this year, but they will attract more long haul, flight and cruise and "all inclusive" passengers -- all of which have a higher sales price and better margins, Crossland said.

"Bookings are very strong for winter and summer," he said. "People are bringing their buying position forward because there were less late deals in the market last year and they are tending to buy the more expensive products as well."
In the UK, where Airtours has a 20 percent market share, summer bookings are 57.2 percent and winter bookings 12.6 percent ahead of last year.
Scandinavia, where the group has a robust 50 percent market share, turned in record pretax profits of 31.5 million stg.
While the key summer season is not on sale yet, winter 1996/97 bookings were a sharp 92 percent ahead of last year, helped by brand repositioning.

The Scandinavian and UK holiday markets are much more mature markets than the highly fragmented Canadian market, which Airtours said suffered difficult trading conditions. More rationalisation there is on the cards, despite a 58.9 percent rise in winter holiday bookings.
But Crossland said Airtours was in an ideal position as the Canadian market comes towards maturity over the next couple of years.
